oneLineAnswer: A prescription tablet for diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome in adults; it eases pain and loose stools, with rare serious risks.
whatItIs: Eluxadoline is a prescription-only medicine sold under the brand name Viberzi. It comes as tablets of 75 mg and 100 mg. In the United States it is a Schedule IV controlled substance, a legal category for medicines the government tracks because they can be misused. It was first approved in the United States in 2015 for adults with irritable bowel syndrome that causes diarrhea. Irritable bowel syndrome is a long-term gut condition with recurring belly pain and changed bowel habits.
whatItDoes: It works on opioid receptors in the wall of the gut. Opioid receptors are docking points that normally respond to the body's own pain-relief chemicals.
It switches on the mu and kappa receptors while blocking the delta receptor. That combination is meant to slow the bowel and settle pain.
The FDA review notes that only a small share of a swallowed dose reaches the bloodstream, so the drug is thought to act mainly inside the gut.
In the two trials that supported approval, people taking it reached a combined target of less belly pain and firmer stools more often than people on placebo.
The FDA reviewers wrote that its clearest measured effect was on stool firmness rather than on pain.
howPeopleUseIt: It is a tablet taken by mouth, and the label says to take it with food.
In the trials that supported approval, adults took it twice daily, for between three months and a year.
Two tablet strengths exist. The label lists the lower strength for people who cannot tolerate the higher one, and for people whose bodies clear the drug more slowly.

commonSideEffects: Constipation is the most common complaint. The label calls it the most frequently reported side effect in the trials.
Nausea and belly pain are also common, and both showed up more often than they did on placebo.
Vomiting, bloating, gas, dizziness and rash each appeared in a few percent of people in the trials.
A mild rise in a liver enzyme reading (ALT) occurred in about 3% of people on the higher strength, against about 1% on placebo.
A small number of people in trials reported feeling drunk or unusually elated.
seriousSigns: Inflammation of the pancreas, called pancreatitis, has been reported. It happened mostly in people who no longer have a gallbladder. Some of those cases were fatal.

The sphincter of Oddi is a valve that controls the flow of bile and pancreatic juice into the first part of the small intestine. That valve can go into spasm, which causes severe pain and can also inflame the pancreas.

Serious allergic reactions have been reported, including anaphylaxis, which is a sudden whole-body reaction. Reported signs were swelling of the face and throat, breathing trouble and chest tightness.
Severe constipation after approval was in some cases followed by a blocked bowel, a hole in the bowel wall, or a hard stool mass that needed treatment.
Most of the serious pancreas and valve-spasm cases in the trials began within the first week of treatment, and some after only one or two doses.
whoShouldAvoid: People who no longer have a gallbladder. The label treats this as a hard stop.
People with a known or suspected blockage of the bile ducts, or with disease or poor function of the sphincter of Oddi.
People with alcohol abuse or addiction, or who drink more than three alcoholic drinks a day.
People with past pancreatitis, or with structural disease of the pancreas such as a suspected blockage of the pancreatic duct.
People who have had an allergic reaction to this medicine before.
People with severe liver disease, graded as Child-Pugh class C. This is a staging system for how well the liver is working. Blood levels of the drug rose about 16-fold in that group.
People with a history of long-lasting or severe constipation, or with a known or suspected physical blockage of the gut.
The label notes that older adults in the trials had more side effects and more serious side effects than younger participants.

interactions: The body clears eluxadoline partly through a liver transporter protein called OATP1B1. Medicines that block that protein, such as cyclosporine, gemfibrozil, rifampin, eltrombopag and some HIV drugs, raise eluxadoline blood levels.
The label warns against pairing it with other medicines that slow the bowel, including opioid painkillers, anticholinergic drugs and alosetron.
Eluxadoline can push up blood levels of rosuvastatin, a cholesterol medicine. The label flags a raised risk of muscle injury from that combination.
Loperamide, a common anti-diarrheal, is listed as something to use only now and then alongside it, not long term.
pregnancyAndChildren: There are no studies of eluxadoline in pregnant women, so the risk during pregnancy is not known. Animal studies in rats and rabbits found no harm to the developing young at high doses. It is not known whether the drug passes into human breast milk, though it does appear in rat milk. Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether it helps other forms of irritable bowel syndrome. It is only approved for the type that causes diarrhea.
How long it stays safe and useful. The trials ran for about three months to a year.
How it compares with other treatments. The trials compared it only with placebo.
The exact share of a swallowed dose that reaches the bloodstream. The label states that absolute bioavailability has not been determined.
Whether it helps children. No pediatric study established that.
Whether it reaches human breast milk.
The true rate of rare harms. Postmarketing reports are voluntary, so counts of reports cannot be turned into a reliable risk rate.
Whether the benefit at six months holds for the lower strength. In one of the two trials the 75 mg result at 26 weeks was not clearly separated from placebo.

gaps: NCCIH has no eluxadoline page; https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/eluxadoline returned a 404, so no NCCIH content is used.

The LiverTox chapter on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov sits behind a bot check and could not be fetched directly. Its summary text was reached only through the PubChem mirror, so no LiverTox-only figures are included.
Two ClinicalTrials.gov API calls returned 400 Bad Request (a phase-filtered query and a nested results-field query). The underlying records were retrieved with simpler queries instead.

MedlinePlus drug monographs were not used because NLM states that content is licensed from the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists and is copyrighted. No MedlinePlus health topic page for eluxadoline was found.
No head-to-head trial against another IBS-D treatment was found, so no comparison of effectiveness can be stated.
Absolute bioavailability is not stated in the label, so how much of a swallowed dose reaches the bloodstream is unknown.
No human data on pregnancy or breast milk exist, and no pediatric data exist.
Independent postmarketing case counts for pancreatitis could not be confirmed from a source that could be fetched, so no such count appears here.
Nothing was found on cost, availability outside the United States, or how long people typically stay on treatment in practice.
summary: This record covers what eluxadoline is, how it acts on gut opioid receptors, what the two pivotal trials measured, its common and serious side effects, who the label excludes, its drug interactions, and the honest gaps around pregnancy, children and rare postmarketing harms.
